cards.b:
Shine light on some metals and electrons fly out. This is the photoelectric effect. It powers light sensors, solar cells and digital camera chips.

It was also the effect that forced Einstein, in 1905, to say something shocking: light itself arrives in packets. That earned him the 1921 Nobel Prize, not relativity.

Heinrich Hertz noticed in 1887 that ultraviolet light helps sparks jump. Philipp Lenard (1902) measured it carefully. Light knocks electrons out of a metal surface. Then came three odd facts.

  1. Below a certain colour (frequency), no electrons come out, however bright the light.
  2. Above it, electrons come out instantly, even with dim light.
  3. Brighter light gives more electrons, but not faster ones. Only a bluer colour gives faster electrons.

If light is a smooth wave, a brighter wave carries more energy and should shake electrons out harder. Dim light should work eventually, just slowly, as the electron soaks up energy like a bucket under a drip. Colour should not matter much.

The data said the opposite: colour decided everything, brightness only the count. The wave picture had no answer.

In 1905 Einstein took Planck's idea seriously: light itself is made of packets, each with energy hf. One packet hits one electron, all or nothing.

The equation in words

Kinetic energy of the electron = packet energy (hf) minus the "work function" W, the fee the metal charges to let an electron go.

Red packets are too small to pay the fee, so no electron escapes, however many red packets arrive. Blue packets can pay, and any extra becomes speed. Brightness only means more packets, so more electrons.

A vending machine wants a 10-rupee coin. Pouring in a thousand 1-rupee coins will not work, but one 10-rupee coin works at once. Colour is the coin size; brightness is how many coins you have.

Where it breaks: a machine can accept several small coins added up. An electron almost never accepts two small photons at once (only in very intense laser light).

Einstein's claim was so strange that Robert Millikan spent about ten years (1914-1916) building careful vacuum experiments to refute it. He measured the electron energy against light frequency and found a straight line exactly as Einstein predicted, and used its slope to get Planck's constant. He admitted the result, and won the 1923 Nobel Prize partly for this.

Then in 1923 Arthur Compton showed X-rays bounce off electrons like billiard balls with definite momentum, so the packets (later named photons) really behave like particles.

Light still shows waves: it makes interference patterns (Young, 1801). So light behaves as a wave when travelling and as lumps when exchanging energy with matter. Modern theory (quantum field theory) says it is neither a classical wave nor a classical ball but something new that shows each face in different experiments.

The honest summary: the mathematics is clear and tested; the plain-language picture is always a compromise.

• "Einstein won the Nobel for relativity." The 1921 prize cited his law of the photoelectric effect.
  • "Brighter light means more energetic photons." No. Brighter means more photons. Energy per photon depends on colour.
  • "Photons are tiny marbles." They have no sharp position when travelling; the particle side shows up only on detection.

C.V. Raman discovered in 1928 that when light scatters from molecules, a little of it comes back with a changed colour. In photon terms, a photon gave some energy to the molecule (or took some) and left with less (or more). That is the Raman effect, announced on 28 February 1928 with K.S. Krishnan; Raman won the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics, the first for an Indian in science. India celebrates 28 February as National Science Day.

Raman spectroscopy is now a standard way to identify materials, and it works because light comes in photons.

• Photoelectric facts: threshold colour, instant action, speed set by colour not brightness.
  • Einstein 1905: light comes in quanta of energy hf. Millikan confirmed it in 1914-16; Compton added momentum in 1923.
  • Raman effect (1928) is photons trading energy with molecules.

Think about it

  1. A very bright red lamp ejects no electrons from a metal, but a faint blue lamp does. Explain with photons.
  2. Why does a solar panel need light above a certain frequency?

quiz.q: What happens if light is below the threshold frequency but very bright?
quiz.w: Each red photon is too weak to pay the work function.

quiz.q: Einstein won the 1921 Nobel Prize for:
o: The law of the photoelectric effect
quiz.w: The citation named the photoelectric law.

quiz.q: Brighter light of the same colour gives:

o: The energy needed to free an electron from the metal
quiz.w: It is the fee the metal charges.

quiz.q: Why did the wave picture fail here?
o: It predicted no light at all
It predicted that brightness controls electron speed and colour is unimportant
quiz.w: The data showed colour mattered most.

quiz.q: Who experimentally tested Einstein's equation in 1914-16?
quiz.w: Millikan wanted to refute it but confirmed it.

o: X-ray photons carry momentum like particles

quiz.q: When did Raman announce his effect?
quiz.w: Raman and Krishnan observed it in 1928; Nobel in 1930.

quiz.q: Why can light still show interference if it is made of photons?
o: Photons show wave behaviour while travelling
quiz.w: Light has both faces depending on the experiment.
